sections.text: In Rust, everything inside a module is private by default. Private means: only code in that module, and in the modules nested inside it, can use the item. To let the outside world in, you add pub.

main can call reveal and peek because they are pub. It cannot call secret directly. The rule of thumb: children can see their parents' private items, but parents and neighbours can't see a child's private items. This lets a module hide its inner workings and show only a small, safe set of functions.
This code does not compile. Rust reports E0603: function `audit` is private.

pub also works on structs, but a struct has two levels. pub struct makes the type public. Each field is still private unless it has its own pub. That is useful: the module can keep a field private and only let outsiders change it through methods that check the rules.

owner is public, so main can read it. balance is private, so main can only use deposit and balance(). Writing acc.balance from main would fail with E0616: field `balance` is private. Notice that Account::new is also needed: main can't build Account { ... } itself, because it can't name the private field. Enums are different. If an enum is pub, all of its variants are public automatically.
Writing long paths gets tiring. The use keyword brings a name into scope so you can use the short form. use only affects the module it is written in, so a nested module needs its own use lines.

Two details. First, as gives an item a new name. std::fmt::Result and std::io::Result are two different types with the same name, so use ... as FmtResult and as IoResult keeps them apart. Second, there is a common habit: bring in types directly (use zoo::animals::Animal), but bring in the parent module for functions (use zoo::show, then show::line). That way a call like show::line shows where the function comes from.

You can group several names from one path with braces: use std::collections::{HashMap, HashSet};. A * (use std::collections::*;) brings in everything public, but it makes it hard to see where a name came from, so it is rare in real code.

If you have used import in Python or JavaScript, use is the same idea. as is like import ... as. The big difference is the default: in Rust the author of a module decides what to share with pub, and everything else stays hidden.

There are finer levels of pub. pub(crate) means visible anywhere inside this crate but not to other crates; pub(super) means visible to the parent module. pub use re-exports a name, so users of your library see a tidier path. These come into play once you write libraries.

exercise.prompt: Make three changes. 1) Add a method pub fn withdraw(&mut self, amount: i64) to Account that subtracts the amount from the balance. 2) Add the line use bank::Account; above main and write Account::new("Ada") instead of bank::Account::new("Ada"). 3) In main, call acc.withdraw(10) right after the deposit. It should print: Ada: 30

quiz.question: If you write an item in a module with no pub, who can use it?
options: Only code in that module and the modules nested inside it
Nobody, not even the module itself

quiz.question: A module has pub struct Account { pub owner: String, balance: i64 }. What can code outside the module do with an Account value?
options: Read owner, but not touch balance directly

quiz.question: What does the as in use std::io::Result as IoResult; do?
options: Gives the imported item a new name
Converts the type to another type
